newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Fleetwood Mac make reuniting fun.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Fleetwood Mac make reuniting fun.

text.p: Twenty years ago, the members of Fleetwood Mac turned painful experiences into blockbuster success with their album "Rumours."

The heady mixture eventually tore the band apart. But now that the bad times are merely bittersweet memories, the quintet has reunited to release its first album in ten years and promote it with a major concert tour.

Lindsey Buckingham, Mick Fleetwood, John and Christine McVie and Stevie Nicks, the best-known incarnation of the veteran band, started rehearsals on April 1. Given that the band consists of two former couples and of people who have struggled with various personal and chemical demons, everything seems to have gone well so far.

"I think we all look back and laugh," keyboardist/singer Christine McVie, 54, said in an interview with Reuters. "So many bottles of wine have been drunk under the bridge since then, and have flown under the bridge as well. We've all pretty much healed from those days."

The last time these five released an album was in 1987 with "Tango in the Night." Nicks, who had beaten a cocaine addiction the year before, was barely involved in the recording; Buckingham, still upset with Nicks over their break-up a decade earlier, opted not to tour behind the album.
In recent years, the mighty franchise had become a self-parody consisting of Fleetwood, the divorced-but-friendly McVies and some hired hands. It dissolved two years ago.
NEW TUNES AND GOLDEN OLDIES

Fleetwood Mac taped three invitation-only concerts at a Warner Bros. soundstage in Los Angeles in May, unveiling four new songs and revisiting chestnuts such as "Rhiannon," "Don't Stop" and "Tusk." The last two featured the 85-strong University of Southern California Trojans Marching band.

"Fleetwood Mac: The Dance," a 90-minute concert special culled from two of those shows, premiered on MTV on Aug. 12 and will be syndicated internationally next month. VH1 will air a behind-the-scenes look at the reunion on Sept. 7.
A companion live album, "The Dance" (Reprise), will be released worldwide on Aug. 19 and the U.S. tour is scheduled to kick off in late September in Boston.

The MTV special and album focus on songs from the 1975 album "Fleetwood Mac," which marked the band debut of Buckingham and Nicks, and the 1977 follow-up "Rumours." The "Fleetwood Mac" album went to No. 3 in U.S. charts. But about this time the McVies were divorcing, Fleetwood's wife ran off with his best friend and Nicks dumped Buckingham after seven years. Nicks later had a brief fling with Fleetwood.

The chaos did provide some good material for "Rumours." Buckingham savaged Nicks in "Go Your Own Way," McVie wrote about her husband in "Don't Stop" and about her new beau in "You Make Loving Fun," and Nicks dealt with bad relationships and cocaine in "Gold Dust Woman."

"Rumours" won the album of the year Grammy in 1977, topped the U.S. charts for 31 weeks, produced four top 10 singles and has sold more than 25 million copies worldwide. Subsequent tours and albums cemented the group's place in rock history. But the inner turmoil never went away.
ANATOMY OF A REUNION

As "flag waver" for the band that he co-founded in 1967, Fleetwood, 55, always hoped his famous five would reunite. The group did sing "Don't Stop" for newly inaugurated President Bill Clinton in 1993 but it was an uncomfortable affair.
"The ironic thing, as with advice for lovers, (is) let go and they'll come back," Fleetwood said backstage after a taping. "I had given up on this happening, but it happened."

The catalyst was a solo album Buckingham started more than a year ago. He and Fleetwood had fallen out a few years earlier but Fleetwood beat a drinking problem and played drums on the project. When the McVies and Nicks came aboard, a formal band reunion was the inevitable outcome.

"I just feel like there's a renewed enthusiasm for being in the band that I certainly didn't have when I left," singer/guitarist Buckingham, 49, said backstage. "Everyone had taken some steps growing-wise."

McVie, now married to musician Eddy Quintela, regards Fleetwood and her former husband, 51, like brothers, and is getting along better with Nicks, 49, than ever before. "Lindsey has really softened up in these last few years," she added. "He's not such a tyrant as he used to be."

The band is scheduled to play 40 dates in the United States and may play in Europe next spring. While Fleetwood would like the band to keep going, Buckingham and McVie are not so sure. He has to finish his record and she had been looking forward to semi-retirement in the English countryside.
"Things are always subject to change in this band," McVie noted resignedly. "You turn one corner and then the whole situation appears in a completely different light."
